utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, too. I see that everyone is here except Mr. Bourgon, as per agreed. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand that there are some preliminaries you need to have dealt with. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to inform you that the Defence of General Miletic joins the Defence of Popovic regarding intercepts, regarding the application made yesterday by the Popovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Any other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. We join, and we also made a filing yesterday afternoon formally sharing the arguments as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That, I'm aware of. All right. Anything else? Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Borovcanin would also join Mr. Popovic's Defence in this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence team wants to stay neutral on this or disassociate itself? Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We take no position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You take no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We stay neutral, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You stay neutral.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are also going to remain neutral on this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've covered everyone, I think; no? Yes, we've covered everyone. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have known that many of the Defences would be challenging the intercepts so that we are -- as any evidence, we will be putting on evidence of their authenticity and their basic chain of custody. I don't believe the Defence, in their motion, are suggesting they have some special legal defence or something of that sort, because, of course, if they did, we should have heard from that long ago. I think they're just talking about basic authentication, basic reliability, as they've stated in the rules. So I think we are all on the same page with that. I don't see or hear any special legal defences or anything like that, and I'm sure we are too late for that. But that's our understanding, and we are fine with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, I don't, respectfully, agree with the Prosecutor. In fact, yesterday or the day before, we received proofing notes regarding this particular witness and new evidence has come forth in connection with whether or not that evidence, indeed, is reliable and authentic. The Prosecutor was kind enough, as is his duty, to share with us that there were alterations and modifications made to certain intercepts, particularly those that involve my client on a certain date that he may testify to. So I don't believe that the issue is necessarily an old one. I think it's ripe for discussion now. However, we thought for the efficiency of the trial that we'll hear the evidence and then bring forth the arguments, as the Popovic Defence team, in their motion, suggested. After you hear all the evidence, it might be a better way to decide whether the evidence should be accepted or not, and if, at all, it is reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may just be a difference of view-point. I don't see any new evidence or anything new, and I don't see alterations. But, of course, we are sharing with the Defence what specifics we learned and how these intercepts are developed, and you'll see the drafts and how the changes become final and all that. And, of course, the Defence views those as alterations; we view them as the process. And we look forward to that disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. May I just point out something which is strictly procedural, and my idea is to draw your attention to it. My colleagues and I are absolutely ignorant as regards the content of the evidence that we will be receiving on these intercepts, and we are also not in a position to know, because that's the system we have adopted, whether, on one particular intercept, there will be just one witness or several witnesses. Like you said, we haven't got an idea on what the various Defence teams are now, or will later be, basing their objection to the admissibility of these intercepts. Of course, as with other things, these are pleasures yet to come and we will be able to take that in due consideration, as it arises. However, may I just make sure to draw your attention to the second paragraph, subparagraph, paragraph (H) of Rule 90, which deals with a special function or responsibility that you have and that you carry as Defence counsel. It's a legacy of the common law tradition; namely, that in cross-examining a witness who is in a position -- "who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." I'm drawing your attention to this because the consequence of failure to attend to this may, although it need not necessarily always lead to that conclusion, one of the consequences may be that there would be a prohibition, later on, on you to raise the matter if you have not contested it with the witness during the cross-examination. It's not an absolute rule. It admits of exceptions. But I think we are in an area where we should alert you to this rule, which is, most of the time, neglected both by some Trial Chambers and by counsel alike. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just briefly give you a little road map, without arguing any of the substantive matters, Mr. President. We have many intercept operators and they are here basically to establish the authenticity, the credibility, the system by which was in place. We will start with supervisors and we will then get to the individual intercept operators who took intercepts related to the accused, as I'm sure you're familiar with. So these intercept operators many times don't know anything about the substance, and so we are not going to be asking them to analyse or evaluate any of the substance, though I'm sure you'll recognise names and things. That, of course, will come later with witnesses, with experts, in that regard. Now, we have just, about a half an hour ago, received a request from one of the Defence counsel for several original notebooks, which you'll be learning about, that they want to use in cross-examination. We are getting those for them, though it's a little late, but hopefully we will be able to get them before cross. Now, this first witness is a supervisor of one of the areas. He has basically one intercept that's part of our evidence, so he'll just be talking about one intercept. But as the supervisor for a larger unit, it's probably fair that he is open for cross-examination, to some degree, about other intercepts that were taken under his watch. Now, you can imagine the mathematical computations of that, if each witness is asked about other intercepts from the ones that they did themselves seven times, so we may need a bit more organisation on the part of everyone to keep that in an area that doesn't keep us here forever. I don't see it as a problem, but we'll wait and do it and see how it comes out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that. Of course, you will have all the cooperation of the Trial Chamber. May I just also remind you that when we were discussing the question of admitting these intercepts and also the testimony of some of the witnesses given in previous cases, having already been put on notice by all of you that intercepts were basically something that you were going to contest, in due course, we made sure that all these witnesses will be present here to give testimony and be available for cross-examination, because that gives you an indication that you will, of course, receive all the necessary understanding and cooperation that both sides require in dealing with this delicate part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we fully understood your holding in that regard. We did go through our collection of intercepts we intended to use and we did find some that, under your ruling, would go to acts or conduct, and so we've had to get and track down the intercept operators that go to those intercepts. That is going to be a motion, kind of, identifying them, that we'll need to call them, too, so that these intercepts that potentially go to acts or conduct are covered by the appropriate witness so they can be cross-examined. So that ruling, we understand it, but we do need to bring in few more people as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Incidentally, how long do you anticipate this witness, this first witness, to be testifying in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm hoping two or three hours, but these guys tend to get into technical stuff that I will try to stop, because I don't understand it. But if -- I don't think more than about two or three hours, Your Honour. I'm hoping I can do it in three hours. But it really -- we'll see how he talks. I haven't done this particular witness before, so I'm not sure. But about three hours is probably a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And is there a first estimate on the part of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you, Mr. President. I think that our cross-examination would take about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An hour, roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Today is Tuesday, so we'll have the whole of tomorrow; that's Wednesday. Could you also, during the first break, try to give the registrar, please, an estimate of the witness to follow. The reason is the following: That Friday, we'll have a Status Conference in the other case at 9.00. We have shifted the time because we need to have a 65 ter meeting at 8.00, enabling us to start that Status Conference at 9.00. Since then, the technicians will require 30 minutes to change, swap tapes, et cetera, we'll start this case at 10.00 on Friday. If that witness who will be testifying on Friday will, in any case, continue testifying on -- finish or continue his testimony on Monday, then we will stop on Friday at the regular time of 1.45. If there is a good chance of finishing with his testimony and sending him home on Friday, our idea was that at 1.45, we'll have a short break and then we will continue again -- we'll have a 30-minute break and then we will continue and finish with his testimony. That was the -- but finishing with his testimony. I did not have in mind having a full afternoon session. I mean, we are talking of maybe half an hour, three-quarters of an hour, but a maximum of one hour and that's about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one final thing: The first two witnesses, the second witness, unfortunately, is the headquarters witness that has the big picture, but because of scheduling and flights and things, he has to go second. The first witness is a supervisor witness. So we'll get the big picture -- the smaller picture before we get the big picture, but it shouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, anyway, give us a bird's eye view, more or less, what you expect; and if your expectations are, maybe after consultations with the Defence team, that this person will still be with us on Monday, then we don't need to go beyond what is basically required of us and we'll stop at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The plan for this first witness is full question and answers. The second witness is partially 92 ter based on some evidence to try to save some time. And then most of the intercept operators, the actual soldiers, we hope to do 92 ter and maybe talk a bit about their individual intercepts, but then try to save as much time as we can in that regard. That's the plan. This first witness, I agreed with the Defence that -- well, I partially agreed with a couple of the Defences that his prior-to-war experience I can read out in a leading way, but they would prefer that when I get to the wartime experience, I go question and answer. So that's fine. That's the way we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. This is delicate terrain, so I mean, the more you agree amongst yourselves, the better it is. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Sorry to turn up like a bad penny, but we've got some business left over from yesterday and it's at the Court's pleasure whether to do it now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do it now. The tendering of documents, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just have two items. The first is P02294, the pseudonym sheet; the second is P02295, and that is the SJB document which was the subject of discussion both on direct and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? None? All right. They are so admitted. Now, Defence teams. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our Defence would like to propose three exhibits: One is the order of the public security centre in Bijeljina of the 14th of July, 1995, we marked as 4D00062. Then the report by the public security centre of Zvornik of the 15th of July, 1995, and that is Exhibit, on 65 ter list, number 4DP00063, or, because it has two markings, 4D500913. And the third document is a statement by (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) that we marked as 4D0063. And just to inform the Trial Chamber that the translations of these two documents are now ready and are already entered into the system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the last of these documents will go under seal. Mr. Stojanovic, you mentioned also one document which has a P number and also A4D number. It's the second one. Registrar, I need your guidance here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can't remain 4D. This is what I wanted to -- all right? So it has to be given the proper protocol number that we have agreed and put in place for Defence exhibits that are also a Prosecution exhibit. Any objections for the tendering of these -- for the admission of these three witnesses, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And no objections from the rest of the Defence teams? They are so admitted. Any further documents you wish to tender as exhibits? None? Mr. Thayer, I thank you so much. Can we bring in the next witness? I think you need to pull down the curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reminded that this person has a voice -- do you mind if I sit down again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not at all, no at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that applies to any of the Defence teams, particularly those who have an imposing stature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in this Srebrenica II case. Our rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn -- you make a solemn declaration with us that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of this the solemn declaration. Please read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the new witness has been admitted into the courtroom. He will be testifying under a pseudonym. He will be referred to as Prosecution Witness 132. He also has been granted two further protective measures, namely, voice and facial distortion. He's taken the oath; he's made the solemn undertaking to testify the truth. Mr. McCloskey is about to start his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have received permission to sit down so that I can make sure I will turn off the mike during our questioning. Now, I first want to go over some background information, and if you can tell me if -- whether or not what I'm saying is true: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, so let's go back to closed session -- to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned ham radios. Do ham radios have any mechanical difference than, say, military radios? And can you just give us a general idea, if there is any difference at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: In principle, there is no difference. Of course, slight differences do exist, which their own name denotes. Ham radio operators work on machinery that is different to that used by the military, given the scope of their activity, although there are machines that are quite similar, by virtue of their technical features. The military equipment, however, is produced for quite specific purposes and weather conditions. They have to meet the most extreme of requirements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we -- I want to go back to your personal background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go back into private for a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness, when you started work, did your work pretty much stay the same through the end of the war, at the location where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. I performed the same duties as in the unit previously. I performed the same duties throughout the war until I got out of the military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll get into the specifics of that a bit later, but was the job you were doing at one site roughly the same job that was going on at the other site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We better go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like for you to continue describing the general process that you got pursuant to orders, and after we're through with the general process, I'll ask you for your specific orders for July 1995, and then we'll go through the process more specifically. But can you continue your explanation of the general process. You said that you directed the antenna to receive certain areas and you would receive certain information. Then what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. If we leave out the orders, our routine work was, once we found a certain direction or a certain location that we were looking for, that we would find the frequencies, in both types of equipment; then we would search for the participants. We would let the equipment intensively scan; some we would scan manually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get into details about that. But, okay, after scanning, what's next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I only stopped because of the interpretation, to give time. After we finished scanning, then the participants would appear, the important conversations would appear, the secret names we would expecting, and then we would continue with the work that we were essentially doing. First, what we would do when we found a conversation is to stop the scanner; then we would press pause -- depress pause and then we would begin to record the conversation. There was an operator for that set or the two sets. He would have the headphones in the same way that I have them now, and the conversation would be recorded to the end. The operator, if it was an easy, short conversation, without a lot of information, could, even in the course of the conversation, note down some things. But what he has to write down at the beginning of every conversation, on a piece of paper, at the side, would be the time, the frequency, and the channel. This information would be used later when transcribing the conversation from the tape to a hard copy. When that part of the work was complete, when the conversation was finished, the operator would switch off the UHER, and then if there was some other activities, he would transfer it to the next conversation. He would move the set to the next set, unless the other set was already doing this work, and then he would begin to transcribe the audio version to the written, hard copy form. So that was the essence of the work that we were doing. The operators had very trained ears. They were used to different kinds of noise; they were used to the voices of the officers that they were monitoring throughout that time-period. They, themselves, had their own routine information which helped them to do this work without too much difficulty. It wasn't always easy, however, to transcribe a conversation. Sometimes you would have interference, something unclear, interruptions, unclear words, all kinds of things. And in such cases, a conversation had to be listened to several times, several times again, even up to ten times. Sometimes we would all gather around and try to see what one word actually was, and believe me, sometimes we didn't succeed in this. We would have to put dots. We wouldn't know what was actually being said in such cases. Sometimes it would happen that people kept replaying the tapes, like DJs. Essentially, when you were transcribing a conversation, you would transcribe two to five -- three to five words, depending on how much a person could remember, but always only as much as you were able to play back the tape by hand; then you would press pause again and then you would replay the tape to see if he was sure about what he had heard, and so on and so forth. That was how we transcribed the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, generally, after it's transcribed, what happens to the material? I'm going to take you through this in more detail with examples of the specific equipment involved, but can you tell us, generally, after the conversation gets transcribed in this way, what happens to the information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I went back to that time. I was just feeling the way I felt at the time. When we transcribed the conversations, we would use the term "skidanje razgovora," taking down the conversation. That was the term that we used. It would refer to the crypto protection room. That's where it would be typed into a computer. The person who brought the message would read it to the person who was operating the encryption equipment, and that's how this would be done. Then grammatical corrections would be entered, nothing more than that. This was the preparation of the text, to put it in a report to our command. That was the form it was sent in to the command. This was the material. Essentially, the material that was brought in was just a draft for something that would later become an official document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us how, if time or any other information was noted in this process, the time of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Time, channel, and later the participants were entered once the conversation was transcribed. These were entered as the title. This was the information that had been entered on that piece of paper. This was a condition to begin transcribing the conversation, because next to that information there was always a number entered, and that number was the counter number on the UHER recorder. It would usually be put on zero. I say zero, because if the conversation -- if there was more than one conversation, it wouldn't be zero. So if it was one conversation, it would go from zero to a certain number; then would you go to that and transcribe it from there. The date would be entered by the computer automatically, in the heading of the report. We submitted reports every day, and as far as I know, the date was automatically entered by the computer at the beginning of each report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, we'll go through the different machines in more detail. We have a break in a few minutes. But let me take you back to early July 1995. Can you tell us, as best you can recall, what were your orders, in terms of where were you supposed to be listening? And, as you've described before, what orders did you get regarding that time-frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Relying on my notebook, and you have copies of that document, all the parties present here have it, the last order that was issued on the 8th of June, 1995, says: "Direct the antennas in the direction of those towns." There is a river also that is mentioned, and also a frequency is mentioned, that it will no longer be that particular frequency but another one that our command would provide. There was also a note based on electronic reconnaissance that I had previously provided. Also, in the field, there was another recommendation for another relay station, and there were some other frequencies from that relay device that were made available to us. And we were supposed to scan others, if there were any. As for the first relay frequencies, we would need to find an active station, with participants that we were interested in, and we were supposed to begin our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which towns, if any, were mentioned in this order? You mentioned towns.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. Zvornik, Vlasenica, and the River Drina were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This might be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session. We'll have a 30-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, I notice the presence of Mr. Vanderpuye amongst the Prosecution team. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed. Thank you. We are in open session, by the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned at the break that your orders were to listen in the direction of Zvornik, Vlasenica and the River Drina. Was this a geographic area that, prior to July of 1995, you had had experience listening to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, just roughly, where was your zone of listening? Where did you folks spend most of your time listening in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: We listened mostly to that area, the area of the Drina Corps. There were other orders, and we listened to Ozren. The two, actually, we listened to most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Drina Corps. So you were aware of that particular enemy corps, I take it. So what other structure did you -- were you trained about or did you learn about, about the VRS in this area, during this general time-frame? What I mean is, can you briefly, without a lot of detail, what did you know about the Drina Corps, what unit it belonged to, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps was made up of several brigades. Firstly, we knew that the headquarters of the Drina Corps was at Vlasenica, and that the brigades making up the Drina Corps was Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, Milici Brigade, Vlasenica Brigade, Sekovici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there other brigades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. There were brigades from other corps, and there were other corps -- or actually, there was the Main Staff, the Supreme Staff, of the army of Republika Srpska at Han Pijesak. Thus, we had a map on which persons from OPP plotted these axes and frequencies on the axes of the relay radio sets of the brigades, the stations, as they were called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said people from OPP helped you identify frequencies, I take it. What's OPP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I apologise, the operations centre, which was stationed at the headquarters of our brigade, and our brigade command was stationed at the headquarters of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say -- your unit, was your unit a brigade or -- we may be getting into translation issues. What would you call your electronic warfare unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: My unit, when it was deployed to its site, was called the platoon, whereas the unit stationed at the command and of which my unit was a part was the company, the Anti-Electronic Warfare Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you become familiar with any personalities, their voices, from the Main Staff or the Drina Corps, during the time-period you were listening to their radio transmissions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Well, you know, sir, when someone introduces himself to you ten or 100 times, you should be able to tell that that's that person the next time. They don't need to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that actually happen at high levels, where the enemy officers would actually do that over the open airways?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely to that doctrine that they stuck, that they should not be introducing themselves by their names and that they should not reveal their locations. And they would, themselves, go against that same procedure and end up introducing themselves as well as the secret location, and we were there to catch these moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2067 on the screen, when we get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think -- I think you said "secret location." Were there any VRS code-names for locations that you were able to learn as you listened to these transmissions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. There were code-names, like, for instance, Panorama, Zlatar, Palma, and such like. There was a certain Badem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you in the past drawn up a list of some of those code-names that you and your unit came to know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the list that we ourselves had up in the unit. We had one such list that was provided to us by our command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you're looking at 65 ter 2067. So when you say Panorama, Zlatar, Palma, Badem, for example, can you tell us, as far as you know, were these the code-names in place in July and August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. They used precisely these names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shouldn't they have -- been supposed to change those at a frequent basis for normal radio practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but you should ask them that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I probably should have asked you: How often do they change their code-names around this July period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Not that often, or almost never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us an example of some of the officers who you got used to listening to that introduced themselves over the airways?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, for instance, Mr. Jokic introducing himself. I remember Zivanovic introducing himself, or someone addressing him. Also, one colonel, I know that he was addressed by someone else who was looking after him. He was quite upset for not having got in touch with him. So there were many such examples of people introducing themselves. They even addressed one another by nicknames sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me take you to more specifics of your work so we can understand some of that. My first question would be, you know, how many rooms did the actual intercepting take part in, where the machines were that you described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: If I understand you well, in how many rooms did we have the machines we worked with? Well, we had one room where we had these intercepting sets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many sets you have, and then we'll get into explaining what is in a set in a more detail. But basically -- sorry, let me ask you this question: How many transmissions or conversations could you record at any one time? What was your maximum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Four conversations could be recorded at one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many could be received at one time for recording, if you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How many -- first of all, how many sets of receiving/recording set-ups did you have in this one room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, now I understand. Four sets, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in July 1995, especially between the time-period of July 6th through about July 20th, can you describe to us how busy the airways were that you were listening to in this area that you've described? And I think a good way to do it is, in a time-period of, roughly, five to ten minutes, can you tell us, on an average - and I know this is rough - but during this busy time, at between five and ten minutes, how many transmission conversations would you hear, not record, but would you actually be aware of were being received, you know, by your sets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The time-period you referred to was, indeed, one where the conversations were numerous. The airways were busy and there were communications on several channels. On average, that time-period was never exceeded; and if it was, then the conversations would be taped one after another. If it so happened that we would be recording all of these conversations simultaneously, then we might have missed something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you tell me, in a time-period of five to ten minutes, what would be a busy number, for you, of conversations that would be received, so we -- just so we can get an idea of what busy is, if you know, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Normally, in such a period of time, there would have occurred one conversation, possibly two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One or two conversations every how many minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Every five to ten minutes. That was when the airways were at their busiest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so during the busy time, when you had these four sets in one room, how many men would be on duty dealing with those sets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Two men were enough to work or handle two sets. Where such need arose, all of us would be there, and there were six or seven of us at the time. There could have been more of us even, because the earlier order says that two groups of five or six persons each should overlap; that they should have eight working days, followed by four rest days. All of this you can find in my notes that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that, you're talking about your notebook that you were using at the time of the event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Believe me, I used the notebook to facilitate my work. I didn't know that it was going to have any significance at a later date. All the official documents should be in the possession of my command, of my headquarters, and they should be able to send them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'd just like to know whether you will be going into this, but the description of what kinds of machines we are talking about; whether they each had its own independent scanning facility and whether the recording facility was incorporated, or whether there was just one scanning apparatus and then various recording machines attached to it. I don't know what. Perhaps you can ask the witness, unless you have this already prepared, in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, there is a pipeline, Your Honour. I have pictures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I do want to get to that pipeline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Another just general issue on working these machines. These men in these shifts, did they travel to and from this mountain top daily, or did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. We had ten-day shifts, which meant that once every ten days, we would come up to the location and ten days later we would leave the location. That was the rotation of the shifts, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If they are ten-day shifts, how many hours in a day would the average operator work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: One operator could work eight hours at the most, and normally not in succession. It all depended on how busy the airways were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 1925, and just let me know when that comes up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to take you to the specifics and the specific machines, what they could do and how they were used. Let me start out the question by -- first, you've mentioned that the antennas get directed. Can you tell us, where were those antennas located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The antennas you refer to were mounted outside the building on a site some 4 to 5 metres away. There were antenna posts somewhere around the corner of the building. And this is where the room, the intercepting room, was located in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we now have on the screen 65 ter 1925, and if you could take that little pen again - I don't know where it's hiding - but take a look at this, and we see at least two, three, boxes on this screen. Could you identify, in order of relevance, each machine by drawing the number on them and telling us, you know, in basic terms, what that machine does.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. I will take the following order: As the signal reached the device, which I will now circle from the antenna we spoke about, this would be the machine number 1, which is of Japanese make, ICOM ICR-100, which is a broadband amateur receiver which could receive three types of signals - amplitude, narrow-band FM and broadband FM. In this case, we used broadband FM, which was the RRU-800 or FM-200. The signal went from this machine into a converter or a mixer. This is the machine number 2 I've just circled. The task of this machine was that the signals received by the receiver from the relay radio frequency, to receive these signals that were modulated with the upper and lower USB and LSB transmission. This is an amplitude from which only one band was selected. Out of these signals, or rather, the converter either increased the frequency or reduced it. In this case, it increased it to a higher level so that the machine number 3 could receive the signal. Now, what is this all about? The machine number 3, which I will now mark, this is the Kent receiver, TS-450 is the make, and I apologise if I mix it up with TS-650. They are very similar and the difference is only in the number. So it can be a mono-bander. Let's say it's 450-S. This is a device that can receive several types of modulations, and the frequency scope is from 30 kilohertz as far as the receiving functions are concerned, because I wouldn't -- I don't want to speak about the transmitting scope. In order to receive signals below the 30 hertz, we had to raise them to a level that would be above zero so that this other machine could receive them and so that we could have all the necessary channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you just, very simply, tell us, machine number 3, what basically could it do with the signals coming from number 2, the converter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: It would scan the frequencies. When we got a ready signal from zero to 150 kilohertz, because a characteristic of the military UNF devices like that, this device had the option of receiving signals of the upper USB range and the lower LSB range also. We modulated the channels, for example, that had 12K connections, and the order they were in there, from one to 12, with one range; then the second set would come with another 12 channels, with a different range from the first device. So if the first device had USB transmission, the second one would have LSB transmission, and this is how they alternated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So is machine number 3 able to scan various radio transmissions that you guys have aimed your aerials at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: It could do even more than that, but we needed two lateral ranges, USB and LSB. If the frequency characteristic was too narrow on the transceiver itself, we had the option of choosing filters to bring it up so that we could make the signals clearer. If it was the case that there was a lot of noise and interference, we would use filters of narrower characteristics so that we would clear the hum from the signal. And the device was quite able to do what we needed it to do. It was a satisfactory device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So if number 3 is scanning the transmissions, that means it's looking for transmissions, looking for conversations; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, it was scanning the channels. And usually - this was not necessarily so, but it did happen usually - we could also hear some sort of a sound in the frequency carrier in this first device, the ICOM. We could hear some trace of something happening, that there should be a channel active somewhere there, with the exception of one thing: We could not then hear that a trace was established. This was only done at the beginning, when the radio relay trace was established, using the broadband frequency modulation, so that the two military stations could establish contact amongst themselves. After that, this device would kick in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You need to slow down a little bit. So when the scanner picked up a transmission -- well, before we get to that, is there a person around these machines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely as it is on the photograph here, the stop was -- well, actually, it was a longer table and the devices were lined up on this table, and the person would be sitting, just as I'm sitting at this desk, in front of the desk where all the devices were. Usually on the left side, if that was the order, you would have the UHER device. That would be the recording device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P023 -- we may come back to that, but let's catch this now. Can you do your number again, PW-132, and right in the right-hand corner is fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I apologise to the Prosecutor, I forgot to say something about scanning, the device. I simply didn't have enough time to say it. I didn't manage to say that the device, while it's scanning, is actually listing the given frequencies. It can do that at a considerable speed. It can make a round of all the channels quite quickly. We would then stop the scanner and then we would continue with the work. This is the explanation that I still had to provide. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be clear, you had four of these sets of these three boxes? In other words, you had four sets of these.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, sir. I should have said it earlier, perhaps. We had two sets like this. Two sets were different, for different purposes, for a different type of radio relay station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did those other two sets do fundamentally the same thing, receive transmissions and scan for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. This set was the RRU-800 and FM-200. We also had stations for RRU-1. These were the stations that only had one channel for transmission, and that is why one scanner like this, the ICOM type. In this case, that was the scanner. We could have put 100 memories there, but we never really needed to put in so many. Our requirements were much, much lower than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we -- I want to leave this picture on. Did we save the one with the circles? It went away to cyberspace somewhere? Okay. Can we bring it back? If we can't, I can -- don't worry about it. But there is one other thing I wanted to ask. Ms. Stewart reminds me that we can't mark anything on it, so we might as well stick with the old one. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the frequencies could come up on the machine which was number 3, the big one in this photo; we are back at 65 ter 1925. You also mentioned earlier, when you were talking about the process generally, that a time came up somewhere. Where did the time of the transmission come up? On any of these machines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The time of transmission appeared on device number 1. That would be the trace carrier. That's what I'm going to call it. The display, after a couple of seconds -- or you could actually push a button and then that's how the time would come up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me, still looking at this little setup, where the UHER recorder would sit in relation to these three devices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I've already said that in this example, it would be on the left side. I know this very well because sometimes you needed to work with both hands, and it was only possible if it was on that side, over there. Why? Because you needed to stop the scanner and depress pause, and you had to do that very quickly, or at the same time, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll get into that. Let's go to the next picture, P02307, and let's go back to our process. Let's say the scanner picks up a transmission. What does the operator do, if anything, to save or to capture that transmission from the scanner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The operator, in order to capture the signal from the scanner, had to stop the scanner, had to depress the pause; that is the left button next to this big button. It would need to depress it. There was another way to do it, but, for technical reasons, this one was preferred, because the other way had one disadvantage. I'm sorry, I'm having some interruption in my headphones. The first one had one disadvantage, and that was if it was used, you would then cut off the UHER electric supply and we would not have the beginning of the text. This was not acceptable to us, so we used this other method that I mentioned, this first version, which was using the pause button. We would use the rubber band more and it would be worn down more, but that was something that we did deliberately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "pause button," you're talking about a pause button on the UHER; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. The device, the UHER-type device that is shown on the picture. That's exactly what the device was that we used to record the conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So let me just try to get this straight. When the scanner picked up a particular conversation, the operator could freeze that conversation on the scanner and capture it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. On this device, on the right-hand side, there is a cable, there is a switch, that was connected to the headphones or the out-socket of the other device that we looked at, device number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Does the operator always wear headphones or is there a speaker he can listen to as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, he could also use a speaker. But also to listen back to the conversation, you would always use the UHER headphones so that you would not bother the others working in the room. And it was much better also, the quality of the sound was much better with the headphones than with the loud-speaker. We also used headphones when we needed to tell exactly which word was being said. And then more of us would listen to the word, we would be replaying it over and over, and we couldn't actually tell at once what was being said. In that case, the loud-speaker was more useful than headphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you take your pen again - you've mentioned the pause button a couple of times - and on this UHER device, can you just put a P for -- I think that's "pause" in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There may be people in the room that don't remember reel-to-reel tape recorders, but are the actual reel-to-reel tapes missing on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We can just see the actual tape recorder. There is no audio tape on there. The tape is not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many centimetres is the diameter of those typical UHER tapes, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what the diameter is, as a technical characteristic, but I know it's a reel of approximately this size of plastic or metal. This device had to have two reels, a full one and an empty one. The full one goes on the left side, when the tape is at the beginning, and then the empty reel is placed on the right-hand side. Then from the left, you need to thread the tape to the right side. On the left side, there is a small spindle and then you would thread the tape there and then you would attach it to the empty reel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you clarify for me, as this machine is sitting there with the other machines in the waiting mode, is the pause button pressed down or is it up? Well, is it down or up, when it's sitting there in the waiting mode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: In the waiting mode, the pause button would be pressed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the play button in the waiting mode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The device in the waiting mode, for play, the button would be up. When the tape was being listened to, then the play button would be pressed down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the record button in the waiting mode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: When recording, the recording button would be pressed down. The only thing that I cannot remember here, and I have to be honest, is whether the recording button and the play button would both have to be pressed during recording. This is something that I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But when the scanner captures a signal and the operator captures that scanner, what, if anything, does he then do to the UHER?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: When the UHER recorded a signal, the UHER would be disconnected in order to be able to plug in the headphones. The other reason would be to actually release the device or disconnect the device from the UHER so that there would be no unwanted background noises and sounds. The counter would be then returned to the given value; it would be zero, usually. I already said when it would be zero and when it wouldn't. Then you would begin to transcribe the conversation, to turn it from an audio record into a hard copy, a written record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what I meant is, when does the operator depress the pause button and begin recording a captured transmission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: When the pause button was depressed, the device would automatically begin to record the conversation. That's how it was set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how soon after the scanner had grabbed a transmission was an operator supposed to be -- supposed to start the recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. As fast as possible, depending on what the individual ability of the operator was. At the same time, he would be using a finger of his right-hand to stop the scanner and using the finger of his left hand to depress the pause. And you can judge for yourself how much time he would need for something like that. I think that this would not take that long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your unit record all conversations that it begins to record like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The command issued instructions as to which conversations or what kinds of conversations didn't need to be monitored. In the beginning, it would return the materials to us and select or simply urge us not to record some kinds of things; that they were superfluous, that they were not of any use for us; and then with time, we, ourselves, also understood what kind of conversations should be recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us just briefly some examples of what would be superfluous and what would be important, based on your orders and your experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I should talk about all of them. For example, it would be types of civilian conversations. Another type would be just the conversation for fun, to make the time pass quickly, just chatting. The third type would be conversation of officers with people who were dear to them, and so on and so forth. These were conversations that did not contain any information that was of significance for us. They wouldn't mention any locations or any names; they wouldn't talk about materiel and equipment, movements of enemies, or any other kind of information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: At the beginning, as I said, there were even interventions by the command. Later, I helped, and after that, they really didn't need anyone to point this out to them. They knew it very well. They, perhaps, knew it better than we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If an operator decided that a conversation was not worth recording, can you briefly describe what he would do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: If the operator caught a conversation, the content of which was not interesting for us, or a part of such a conversation, he would automatically have some of it recorded on the tape. Then the operator could stop the tape and wait for a favourable moment to see if the course of the conversation would change, if something would be mentioned after all. And at the end of the conversation, he would rewind the tape to its starting position and then he would tape a new conversation on top of that conversation, a conversation that would be of importance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back into open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happens -- if the conversation appears to be an interesting or a relevant conversation, what does the operator do in that situation? Can you just set out the process, especially as it relates to what you've talked about before briefly, the time, the frequency notations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The operator would first take the headphones which were separately attached to the UHER, so the operator had headphones for the radio receiver, for the radio, as well as the UHER. He would rewind the conversation to its beginning, using the counter, and then when he began to note it down in the notebook, he would first jot down the numbers from the piece of paper where the time, the counter number were noted down, the beginning and the end position of the counter, the frequency, and the channel. Yes, time, frequency and the channel. Then he would leave room for a heading, if he still didn't know who the participants were and which would -- he would then find out in the course of the conversation itself. If it was something that made him believe it was an important conversation, then he would know who the participants were because the course of the conversation was clear. If this was not clear, he would leave that for later. He would then begin to transcribe the conversation. He would press the play button.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You mentioned two things. One, you mentioned a piece of paper and then you mentioned a notebook. I think you've talked about this a bit in your testimony, but just to be clear, let's go back to this piece of paper. What is the significance of this piece of paper? What is done with that, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The piece of paper was used to jot down information, such as the counter number, the time, the frequency, the channel and -- no, not the participants, I'm sorry. This information was later, because it could happen that it was not -- if it happened that it was not an important conversation, you could just simply cross it out. If the conversation was important, then you would enter this information into the notebook. The next thing would be the content of the conversation; that would be recorded word by word, or as much as the operator could remember of what was said. If he had time, then he could write it down. He would press pause. He would write down what he memorised, if something was not clear or if he felt he had made a mistake, he would rewind that section again, and then he would keep going like that, pressing and depressing the pause and taking down a few words at a time. They could jot down at least five words until the next time the text was stopped. And that is how they transcribed the conversation to the end. Usually, if they didn't already put the participants in, they would do that at the end of the conversation, and then they would also indicate which speaker was saying what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just getting you back to that piece of paper, at what point in the conversation that's being recorded does the operator -- is the operator supposed to write down the time of the recording? Excuse me, the time of the transmission or conversation. When, in that process of recording the transmission, is the operator supposed to write down the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Shortly after stopping the scanner and depressing the pause button, the first/next thing the operator was supposed to do was to cast a glance on the monitor of the small device where the signal was received, to look at the time that was there. He had a piece of paper handy. He would first enter the time; then the frequency. As the frequency did not change that often on the carrier, one knew which frequency it was. If not, then one had to press the button, the time button; then you would see the frequency and then it would go back to time. Then you would look at the channel, which could be seen on the device number 3, and that was important. The counter was always on zero or on the point reached. The information was very important for us, because if it happened that we needed to start recording the very next conversation, in order to be able to distinguish between the two conversations, although one could glean that in other ways as well, in case it turned out that one of a series of conversations turned out to be a priority for the command and had to be urgently tracked down - it so happened on several occasion that we had to go back and select some of the conversations - this would be the way to facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How important was accuracy in this process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Very important, because we never knew what was to happen at the next moment. There was general uncertainty with regard to that. We never knew the character and the significance of some of the conversations for our command. That was why we tried to do that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you mentioned transcription and you mentioned notebook. Can you, first of all, describe to us what this notebook looked like and where it fit in in the transcription process.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: The notebook was of the A4 format; I believe that's what the format is. It's a small notebook. There are larger ones, A4 format notebooks. And these A4 format notebooks had 56 sheets and cardboard covers, flexible cardboard covers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were done with these notebooks, just to make it clear, in terms of the recorded conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: In the event a notebook was filled and had no more blank sheets, we, or rather, I would actually store them away in the safe. And I waited for my shift to take this notebook and I would take a different notebook that I received from the command. As soon as one notebook was filled, another one was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this may be my fault, but is it fair to say that the conversation that the operator is listening to is transcribed down into this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This last exhibit, let's get this -- you've made one marking on it, so if you could put, again, "PW-132" and I think we'll send it on its way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we had this piece of paper that you've written -- somebody's written the time and the frequency on, and we have the notebook where the conversation is being transcribed. What's done with the information on this little -- on this other piece of paper, the time and frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you spoke of both the notebook and the piece of paper. Once the information was in the notebook, this meant that the piece of paper was no longer needed. Once the piece of paper is filled up, and all the information contained in it crossed out, we would throw it away, because once we crossed out the information on the piece of paper, that meant that the information had been entered into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it the operator that takes the time and frequency from the piece of paper and puts it in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: I believe I said so. If I did not, let me say that the first thing one did was to copy the information contained on the piece of paper, because that was the starting point - time, frequency, channel, then participants, if known, as a heading; if not, then one first listens to the conversation and subsequently enters the participants. From the point one of the participants introduces himself, then he gets a name. If the participant does not introduce himself through to the end of the conversation, then he remains person X to us. And then if there are several unknown persons, they are marked as person X, Y, Z, and so on and so forth, by using the signs that are unknowns. When the person introduces himself or herself, then, normally, the name of the person, the rank or any other designation, is placed before the text uttered by the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And with that and your other descriptions of the transcription process, I'll leave that subject alone for now. But can you tell us, in the -- is there any sort of policy or practice about how many conversations an operator would transcribe in one sitting? Or can you -- let me start over again, just to make this clear. After an operator finishes transcribing a conversation in the notebook, as you've described in detail how that's done with the other members sometimes, what happens to that conversation? Where is its next stop? And I think you've roughly described that, but if you could, in particular, describe, where does that handwritten conversation go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Once the operator transcribes the conversation, he takes it to the adjacent room, which was KZ room, the room for crypto protection or encryption. There was one computer there, and it was either a 386 or a 486 at the time. It was connected to a network modem, to a telephone line. Through the network, the reports and any other requests we had for our command and any other types of communications went across the computer. As soon as the operator went into that room, he started reading the text out, and the KZ person would type the text up on the computer. If such texts were not a priority, then several of them would make up a report, a regular report, or actually only a part of a regular report, that part which was sent daily from that building to the command, because there were other matters contained in such reports in addition to the texts that we transcribed. These were pieces of information concerning personnel, needs, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, if we need to go into private session, we'll do this. But this location where he operated from, together with the others, was it -- I assume that it had regular electricity and telephone line supplies. Was it an inhabited area? And if it did not always have electricity and telephone connection, when were those services introduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me break that down a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, this mountain top, with this building that you've described, can you describe what else, if anything, was anything around there so we can get a feel for the habitation or lack thereof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: At that location, there was this building which was isolated from the inhabited area. However, in terms of electricity supplies, this building had its own transmission tower and there was this one line, a cable, which carried electricity supplies from the nearest inhabited area to that building. We had regular electricity supplies, for the most part. There were electricity outages and interruptions, either for weather circumstances or any other reasons, in which case we used a generator. We had our generator which we mostly used to charge our batteries, and partly for lighting, for our TV sets, in order to have as normal a life as possible. We had two times 180-ampere-hour batteries, they were large ones, and we had one charger charging the batteries. Since our work did not allow for us to have electricity supplies directly from the grid, all of our devices, since we had the possibility, were connected to the batteries so that in the event of the electricity supplies being cut off, we, or rather, our devices would not suffer in any way. Whenever the electricity was down, we were able to endure the situation for two or even three days without the generator being put to use. We would use the generator where appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the telephone communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We had a constant ATC line, as it was called, which connected us with the nearby town and provided constant contact with the headquarters of our unit. If it so happened that this line should, in any way, be disrupted, we had a radio set which sent our material, as it were, from our computer at the base to the command, to the headquarters. We had a planned frequency which we used for that purpose, and that was used at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the ATC line, is that a hard-wire line you're talking about, no radio waves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a direct telephone line with the nearby town. Beyond our building, there was a barracks, a military facility, which had direct cable lines, and the line was laid down directly from that particular facility all the way to our building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you're running on your batteries, are your four sets of machines at all minimised, or are you able to run at full capacity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: There was no need for reducing our capacity because of problems in power supplies. However, if our activities were not that busy, if we had one to two conversations in an hour or one to two conversations in a day, then we could minimise our working capacities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you back to where we were. We were at -- the operator had taken the notebook to what you've called the KZ man at the computer, who has this -- I think, types up the material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. Typed up, well, I don't know how to -- maybe I should explain this. The person typed up the text dictated by the operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe -- was there any communication between the two or any more editing going on at that point, or was this just dictation and typing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: But, of course, they were human beings and it was natural for them to communicate. I have to get back, again, to saying that the notebook was only a draft, not a finished product. And they would consult one another about a full point being put there or whether this was really a pause or whether the full stop should be taken away, whether this was an entire sentence or whether the person uttered an exclamation, and then they would consult each other about putting an exclamation mark. This was just an illustration of what may have been going on. At the operator's discretion, the KZ man was able to put a full stop where there was none before, based on their consultation. This is something that would be done and could be seen on a finished text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we are okay for a bit. Thank you, Mr. President. I tend to forget that, but I think this is okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were beginning to describe to us, very briefly, but this important job of, I think you called it, electronic reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I called it. It's the task of searching the area, the frequencies, of both radio relay stations, both types of stations. During day-time activities of powerful transmitters that were in the same area, you could conceal a lot of the signals, so that was an ideal opportunity for that kind of work. Sometimes it would happen that some relay stations received adequate substitutes in a certain sector, or rather, they would be prepared for some future activities of those who were using them. Then they would establish relay routes, and it would be very important for us to know when this would happen. A multi-channel type of radio relay station is something that each one had a kind of individual recognition signal, whether this was in the bearer beam, whether it was some kind of interference or a buzz or a pilot carrier, which was very characteristic, and that would help us to recognise if it was a signal of something else or of the radio relay station. Electronic reconnaissance is very important due to the fact that, at a given moment, it could either disappear or stop. The relay station could stop or disappear and then we would lose our material that we were supposed to obtain. That is why we had these frequencies that we had established earlier, and then we would scan them immediately and start our searches so that in plenty of cases we were quite successful in this. This would usually happen before the start of combat actions. One relay station would just go out and appear in a different place and begin with its activities. It would even happen that we would hear the first signal that would be the announcement of the attack, with a specific code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, let me get back to our process, briefly. You had mentioned before, and I don't want you to go over it again, but that during, I think it was, the typing process, that the date got automatically entered by the computer. Did the date of the intercept ever get noted in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Closed Session]
utterances.text: It could happen, but it wasn't necessarily so. Sometimes it could have been noted in the notebook, but this is not something that the command asked us to do, because the whole work would finish with the daily reports or other reports in the course of the day that were not necessarily daily reports. You would enter the date there and then it would become important in the sense that it was put in relation to a certain date, when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to take you to the 14th of July and ask you about a particular conversation that we have a transcription of, both in the typed version and in the handwritten version, and I'd like for you to help us understand it a bit; I am meaning the process and some of the information that's in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could go to 65 ter number 1164E, which should have -- and we need to make sure that this is not broadcast publicly because it has information on it that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if need be, let's go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
